docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
minevent is a Python library that provides a minimal event system for Machine Learning. It allows you to customize code by adding pieces of code that are executed when an event is fired. minevent is organized around three main concepts:

  • event which defines the thing that should happen.
  • event handler which is the piece of code to execute when the event happens
  • event manager which is responsible to manage the events and event handlers.

The goal of this documentation is to explain how the event system works and how to use it. The library provides some implemented modules, but it is possible to extend it. It is possible to use all the components or just a subset based on the need. For example, an event handler can be used without the event manager.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
minevent provides a minimal event system to customize a piece of code without changing its implementation. Below is an example on how to use minevent library.

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def say_something(manager: EventManager) -> None:
...     print("Hello, I am Bob!")
...     manager.trigger_event("after")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> say_something(manager)
Hello, I am Bob!
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("after", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> say_something(manager)
Hello, I am Bob!
Hello!

It allows you to customize the function say_something without changing its implementation. Please read the quickstart page to learn more about the library.

docs.title: API stability
docs.text: While minevent is in development stage, no API is guaranteed to be stable from one release to the next. In fact, it is very likely that the API will change multiple times before a stable 1.0.0 release. In practice, this means that upgrading minevent to a new version will possibly break any code that was using the old version of minevent.

docs.title: Architecture and Design Principles
docs.text: This document describes the architecture and design principles of minevent.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
These properties hold for every release and each one is covered by tests.

  • Events are strings. An event name is a case-sensitive str; any other type raises a TypeError. Reading the manager never creates an event.
  • A registration is a Subscription. add_event_handler returns a new one every time, even for a handler that is already registered. remove() removes that registration only, and returns False when it was already removed.
  • Registration order. The handlers of an event run in the order they were registered.
  • Snapshot dispatch. trigger_event runs the handlers registered when it starts. A handler added or removed by a running handler takes effect at the next trigger.
  • Fail-fast. An exception of a handler propagates to the caller and the remaining handlers are skipped.
  • once is at most once. The registration is removed before the handler is called, atomically, so the handler runs at most once whatever the number of threads. It is consumed even if the condition is false or the handler raises.
  • Synchronous by default. trigger_event never awaits; a handler that returns an awaitable raises a TypeError. atrigger_event awaits the handlers one after the other.
  • Thread-safe registry. Handlers and conditions run outside the lock, so a handler can use the manager.
  • Payload is data. The keyword arguments of trigger_event are passed to every handler, and any key is allowed.
  • No global state. There is no default manager and no discovery.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
minevent is designed as a minimal event system with three core components:

  1. Events - String identifiers representing things that happen
  2. Event Handlers - Code that executes when events occur
  3. Event Manager - Coordinator that manages handlers and triggers events

docs.title: 1. Simplicity First
docs.text:
minevent prioritizes simplicity over features:

  • Minimal API surface area
  • Easy to understand and use
  • No complex configuration required
  • Clear separation of concerns

Example: Events are simply strings, not complex objects.

# Simple and clear
manager.trigger_event("training_complete")

# Not: complex event objects
# manager.trigger_event(Event(name="training_complete", priority=1, ...))

docs.title: 2. Synchronous by Design
docs.text:
trigger_event is synchronous:

  • Handlers execute in the order they were registered
  • Easy to reason about execution flow
  • Simpler debugging and testing
  • Coroutine handlers are opt-in with atrigger_event
  • The registry is protected by a lock, but the library starts no thread

Rationale: ML workflows are often sequential and benefit from deterministic execution order.

docs.title: 3. Explicit Over Implicit
docs.text:
All actions are explicit:

  • Must explicitly register handlers
  • Must explicitly trigger events
  • Must explicitly pass arguments to handlers

Example:

# Explicit registration
manager.add_event_handler("event", EventHandler(handler))

# Explicit triggering
manager.trigger_event("event")

# Not: implicit auto-registration or magic discovery

docs.title: 4. Extensibility Through Composition
docs.text:
Extend functionality by composing handlers and conditions:

  • Base classes for custom implementations
  • An EventHandler combines a handler and an optional condition
  • No inheritance-heavy design

Example:

# Compose handlers with conditions
handler = EventHandler(my_function, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=5))


# Custom conditions: any function without argument that returns a bool
class MyCondition:
    def __call__(self) -> bool:
        return custom_logic()

docs.title: 5. Zero Magic
docs.text:
No hidden behavior or surprising actions:

  • No global state
  • No automatic discovery
  • No metaclasses and no discovery; the only introspection is the optional filter_payload (signature of the handler) and the check of an awaitable result
  • What you write is what happens

docs.title: Event
docs.text:
Design: Events are represented as case-sensitive strings.

Rationale:

  • Simple and universal
  • Easy to type and understand
  • No serialization issues
  • Language-agnostic concept

Best Practices:

  • Use descriptive names
  • Follow consistent naming convention
  • Consider hierarchical naming for complex systems

docs.title: Event Handler
docs.text:
Design: Handlers wrap callable functions with optional arguments.

Class Hierarchy:

BaseEventHandler (abstract)
    ├── EventHandler (handler + arguments + optional condition)
    └── [Your custom handlers]

Key Methods:

  • handle(): Execute the handler logic
  • ahandle(): Execute the handler logic in a coroutine (calls handle() by default)

Rationale:

  • Separation between handler logic and handler metadata
  • Handlers are compared by identity; a Subscription identifies a registration
  • Supports both simple and complex use cases

docs.title: Event Manager
docs.text:
Design: Central coordinator using a dictionary to map events to handler lists.

Internal Structure:

{
    "event1": [handler1, handler2, handler3],
    "event2": [handler4, handler5],
    # ...
}

Rationale:

  • Simple dictionary lookup for handlers
  • Preserves registration order
  • Easy to implement and understand

Key Operations:

  • O(1) handler registration
  • O(n) event triggering (n = number of handlers)
  • O(n) handler lookup (n = total handlers)

docs.title: Conditional Execution
docs.text:
Design: EventHandler can wrap a handler with a condition.

Architecture:

EventHandler(condition=...)
    ├── Handler (callable)
    └── Condition (callable that returns a bool)

Execution Flow:

trigger_event()
    ├── Get handlers for event
    └── For each handler:
        ├── If the handler has a condition:
        │   ├── Evaluate condition
        │   └── If True: execute handler
        └── Else: execute handler

Rationale:

  • Separates "what" (handler) from "when" (condition)
  • Conditions are reusable across handlers
  • Conditions can maintain state between evaluations

docs.title: Registration Flow
docs.text:
1. User creates EventHandler
   EventHandler(function, args, kwargs)

2. User registers handler
   manager.add_event_handler("event", handler)

3. Manager stores handler
   the handler is appended to the list of the event

docs.title: Triggering Flow
docs.text:
1. User triggers event
   manager.trigger_event("event")

2. Manager gets handlers
   handlers = a snapshot of the list of the event

3. Manager executes each handler
   for handler in handlers:
       handler.handle()

docs.title: Handler Execution
docs.text:
Without condition:
    handler(*handler_args, **handler_kwargs, **payload)

With a condition:
    if condition():
        handler(*handler_args, **handler_kwargs, **payload)

docs.title: Custom Event Handlers
docs.text:
Implement BaseEventHandler:

class MyEventHandler(BaseEventHandler):
    def handle(self, /, **payload: object) -> None:
        # Custom logic; payload holds the keyword arguments of trigger_event
        pass

Use Cases:

  • Handlers with complex state
  • Handlers that modify themselves
  • Handlers with special lifecycle

docs.title: Custom Conditions
docs.text:
A condition is any function without argument that returns a boolean (the Condition protocol). Implement __call__ in a class when the condition has a state:

class MyCondition:
    def __call__(self) -> bool:
        # Custom logic
        return some_condition

To combine conditions, write a function: lambda: a() and b() skips b when a is False, and lambda: all([a(), b()]) evaluates both.

Use Cases:

  • Time-based conditions
  • State-based conditions
  • Metric-threshold conditions
  • Complex multi-condition logic

docs.title: Thread Safety
docs.text:
Status: EventManager protects its registry with a reentrant lock. Registering, removing and inspecting handlers, and triggering events, can be done from several threads.

Guarantees:

  • trigger_event runs the handlers of a snapshot taken under the lock; the handlers run outside the lock, in the calling thread, so a handler can use the manager.
  • Handlers added or removed during a trigger take effect on the next trigger.

Not guaranteed:

  • Handlers triggered from several threads run concurrently. A handler that shares state must protect it.
  • The state of a condition (for example the counter of PeriodicCondition) is not protected, so a stateful condition should be triggered from one thread.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
minevent stays minimal. These features are not provided and are not planned:

  • Event objects with metadata or priorities: events are plain strings, and data is given as keyword arguments to trigger_event.
  • Handler ordering other than the registration order.
  • Weak references or sender/receiver filtering.
  • Collecting handler errors: handlers run fail-fast, and an exception stops the dispatch. To run every handler and report all the failures, wrap the handler in a try/except (an ExceptionGroup option such as on_error="collect" was considered and declined to keep trigger_event minimal).

docs.title: Why Strings for Events?
docs.text:
Alternatives Considered:

  • Enum types
  • Custom Event classes
  • Integer IDs

Chosen: Strings

Reasons:

  • Universal and simple
  • Easy to understand
  • No import dependencies
  • Flexible naming
  • Human-readable

docs.title: Why Synchronous by Default?
docs.text:
Alternatives Considered:

  • Async/await support
  • Threading
  • Multiprocessing

Chosen: Synchronous trigger_event, with atrigger_event for coroutine handlers

Reasons:

  • Simpler to understand
  • Easier to debug
  • Deterministic execution
  • Sufficient for ML workflows
  • Coroutine handlers are opt-in with atrigger_event; trigger_event stays synchronous

docs.title: Why Explicit Event Manager?
docs.text:
Alternatives Considered:

  • Global event bus
  • Singleton manager
  • Module-level functions

Chosen: Explicit manager instance

Reasons:

  • No hidden global state
  • Easier to test
  • Multiple managers possible
  • Clear ownership
  • Explicit is better than implicit

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
minevent is designed to be:

  • Simple: Easy to learn and use
  • Explicit: No surprises or magic
  • Extensible: Customize through composition
  • Focused: Does one thing well
  • Reliable: Well-tested and documented

The architecture supports these goals while remaining flexible enough for diverse use cases in machine learning and beyond.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text: This guide provides recommendations for using minevent effectively in your projects.

docs.title: Use Clear, Descriptive Names
docs.text:
Event names should clearly describe what happened or will happen:

# Good
manager.trigger_event("training_epoch_completed")
manager.trigger_event("model_checkpoint_saved")
manager.trigger_event("validation_started")

# Less clear
manager.trigger_event("event1")
manager.trigger_event("done")
manager.trigger_event("x")

docs.title: Use Consistent Naming Conventions
docs.text:
Choose a naming convention and stick to it throughout your project:

# Option 1: Snake case with verb in past tense
"training_started"

"epoch_completed"
"validation_finished"

# Option 2: Namespace-style with present tense
"training.start"
"training.epoch.complete"
"validation.finish"

docs.title: Use Hierarchical Event Names
docs.text:
For complex systems, use hierarchical naming to organize events:

# Training lifecycle
"training.start"

"training.epoch.start"
"training.batch.start"
"training.batch.end"
"training.epoch.end"
"training.end"

# Model lifecycle
"model.created"
"model.compiled"
"model.saved"

docs.title: Keep Handlers Focused
docs.text:
Each handler should do one thing well:

# Good: Separate handlers for separate concerns
def log_metrics(metrics):
    logger.info(f"Metrics: {metrics}")


def save_checkpoint(model, epoch):
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), f"checkpoint_epoch_{epoch}.pt")


def update_progress_bar(current, total):
    progress_bar.update(current / total)


# Less ideal: One handler doing multiple things
def do_everything(model, metrics, epoch, current, total):
    logger.info(f"Metrics: {metrics}")
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), f"checkpoint_epoch_{epoch}.pt")
    progress_bar.update(current / total)

docs.title: Handle Exceptions Gracefully
docs.text:
Protect your main logic from handler failures:

from minevent import EventHandler


def safe_handler(*args, **kwargs):
    try:
        # Your handler logic
        process_data(*args, **kwargs)
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Handler failed: {e}")
        # Optionally re-raise if critical
        # raise


handler = EventHandler(safe_handler)

docs.title: Use Type Hints
docs.text:
Make your handlers more maintainable with type hints:

from typing import Dict, Any


def log_metrics(metrics: Dict[str, float], epoch: int) -> None:
    """Log training metrics for the current epoch.

    Args:
        metrics: Dictionary of metric names to values
        epoch: Current training epoch number
    """
    logger.info(f"Epoch {epoch}: {metrics}")


handler = EventHandler(log_metrics, handler_kwargs={"metrics": {"loss": 0.5}, "epoch": 1})

docs.title: Centralize Event Manager Creation
docs.text:
Create the event manager in one place and pass it where needed:

# Good: Create once, pass around
def main():
    manager = EventManager()
    setup_handlers(manager)
    trainer = Trainer(manager)
    trainer.train()


def setup_handlers(manager: EventManager):
    manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", EventHandler(save_checkpoint))
    manager.add_event_handler("training_end", EventHandler(log_summary))


# Avoid: Global event manager
# MANAGER = EventManager()  # Global state can be problematic

docs.title: Check Before Adding Duplicate Handlers
docs.text:
Prevent duplicate handler registrations by looking at the registrations of the event:

# Add handler only if not already present
handler = EventHandler(my_function)
if not any(sub.event_handler is handler for sub in manager.get_subscriptions("my_event")):
    manager.add_event_handler("my_event", handler)

docs.title: Clean Up When Done
docs.text:
Reset or properly dispose of event managers when they're no longer needed:

try:
    # Training loop
    trainer.train(manager)
finally:
    # Clean up
    manager.reset()

docs.title: Use Conditions for Periodic Operations
docs.text:
For operations that shouldn't happen every time:

from minevent import EventHandler, PeriodicCondition

# Save checkpoint every 10 epochs
save_handler = EventHandler(save_checkpoint, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=10))
manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", save_handler)

# Log metrics every 100 batches
log_handler = EventHandler(log_batch_metrics, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=100))
manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", log_handler)

docs.title: ML Training Pipeline Pattern
docs.text:
class Trainer:
    def __init__(self, model, manager: EventManager):
        self.model = model
        self.manager = manager

    def train(self, epochs: int, train_loader, val_loader):
        self.manager.trigger_event("training_start")

        for epoch in range(epochs):
            self.manager.trigger_event("epoch_start")

            # Training
            train_loss = self._train_epoch(train_loader)
            self.manager.trigger_event("training_epoch_end")

            # Validation
            val_loss = self._validate(val_loader)
            self.manager.trigger_event("validation_epoch_end")

            self.manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")

        self.manager.trigger_event("training_end")

    def _train_epoch(self, train_loader):
        for batch in train_loader:
            self.manager.trigger_event("batch_start")
            loss = self._process_batch(batch)
            self.manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
        return loss

docs.title: Plugin System Pattern
docs.text:
class PluginManager:
    """Manage plugins using event system."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.event_manager = EventManager()
        self.plugins = []

    def register_plugin(self, plugin):
        """Register a plugin and its event handlers."""
        self.plugins.append(plugin)
        plugin.setup(self.event_manager)

    def trigger(self, event: str, **kwargs):
        """Trigger event with data."""
        # Store kwargs somewhere accessible to handlers
        self.event_manager.trigger_event(event)


# Plugin implementation
class LoggingPlugin:
    def setup(self, manager: EventManager):
        manager.add_event_handler("model_trained", EventHandler(self.log_training_complete))

    def log_training_complete(self):
        print("Training completed!")

docs.title: Callback System Pattern
docs.text:
class CallbackSystem:
    """Wrap minevent for a cleaner callback API."""

    def __init__(self):
        self._manager = EventManager()

    def on(self, event: str, callback, condition=None):
        """Register a callback for an event."""
        if condition:
            handler = EventHandler(callback, condition=condition)
        else:
            handler = EventHandler(callback)
        self._manager.add_event_handler(event, handler)

    def emit(self, event: str):
        """Emit an event."""
        self._manager.trigger_event(event)


# Usage
callbacks = CallbackSystem()
callbacks.on("training_complete", send_notification)
callbacks.on("checkpoint", save_model, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=10))

docs.title: Test Event Handlers Independently
docs.text:
def test_handler():
    """Test handler logic without event manager."""
    # Arrange
    handler = EventHandler(my_function, handler_args=("test",))

    # Act
    handler.handle()

    # Assert - verify expected behavior
    assert expected_result == actual_result

docs.title: Mock Event Handlers in Tests
docs.text:
from unittest.mock import Mock


def test_event_system():
    """Test event system with mock handlers."""
    manager = EventManager()
    mock_handler = Mock()

    manager.add_event_handler("test_event", EventHandler(mock_handler))
    manager.trigger_event("test_event")

    mock_handler.assert_called_once()

docs.title: Test Event Flow
docs.text:
def test_training_events():
    """Test that training triggers expected events."""
    manager = EventManager()
    events_triggered = []

    def track_event(event_name):
        events_triggered.append(event_name)

    manager.add_event_handler("start", EventHandler(track_event, ("start",)))
    manager.add_event_handler("end", EventHandler(track_event, ("end",)))

    # Simulate training
    manager.trigger_event("start")
    manager.trigger_event("end")

    assert events_triggered == ["start", "end"]

docs.title: Minimize Handler Count
docs.text:
Too many handlers can slow down event triggering:

# Good: One handler for related operations
def batch_operations(batch):
    log_batch(batch)
    update_metrics(batch)
    check_conditions(batch)


manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", EventHandler(batch_operations))

# Less efficient: Multiple handlers for small operations
# manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", EventHandler(log_batch))
# manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", EventHandler(update_metrics))
# manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", EventHandler(check_conditions))

docs.title: Use Conditional Handlers for Infrequent Operations
docs.text:
Don't execute expensive operations every time:

# Good: Only save checkpoint periodically
manager.add_event_handler(
    "epoch_end", EventHandler(save_checkpoint, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=10))
)

# Less efficient: Save every epoch when not needed
# manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", EventHandler(save_checkpoint))

docs.title: Profile Handler Performance
docs.text:
Identify slow handlers:

import time


def profiled_handler(*args, **kwargs):
    start = time.time()
    actual_handler(*args, **kwargs)
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    if elapsed > 0.1:  # Log if takes more than 100ms
        logger.warning(f"Handler took {elapsed:.2f}s")

docs.title: Avoid Modifying State During Event Triggering
docs.text:
# Surprising: a handler removed during a trigger still runs in that trigger
def remove_other(subscription):
    subscription.remove()


# Better: remove the registration after the event triggering is complete
subscriptions_to_remove = []


def safe_handler(subscription):
    subscriptions_to_remove.append(subscription)


# Clean up after event triggering is complete
for subscription in subscriptions_to_remove:
    subscription.remove()

docs.title: Don't Rely on Execution Order Across Events
docs.text:
# Problematic: Assuming event order
manager.trigger_event("event1")
manager.trigger_event("event2")
# Handlers for event1 and event2 may have side effects,
# but don't assume event1 handlers complete before event2 triggers

# Better: Use explicit ordering within the same event
manager.add_event_handler("event", EventHandler(step1))
manager.add_event_handler("event", EventHandler(step2))  # Runs after step1

docs.title: Avoid Circular Event Triggering
docs.text:
# Problematic: Handler triggers the same event
def recursive_handler(manager):
    manager.trigger_event("my_event")  # This creates infinite recursion!


# Better: Use different events or add guards
def safe_handler(manager, depth=0):
    if depth > 0:
        return
    # Do work
    manager.trigger_event("next_event")

docs.title: What is minevent?
docs.text: minevent is a minimal, lightweight event system for Python, designed specifically with Machine Learning workflows in mind. It provides a simple way to add extensibility to your code by allowing you to register event handlers that execute when specific events are triggered.

docs.title: Why should I use minevent?
docs.text:
minevent is useful when you want to:

  • Add hooks or callbacks to your code without modifying its core logic
  • Implement plugin-like functionality
  • Separate concerns in your ML training pipelines
  • Create extensible frameworks
  • Add logging, monitoring, or debugging capabilities without cluttering your main code

docs.title: How is minevent different from other event systems?
docs.text:
minevent is designed to be minimal and focused. It:

  • Has minimal dependencies (only requires coola)
  • Is synchronous by design (simpler reasoning about execution order)
  • Provides conditional event handling out of the box
  • Is specifically tailored for ML workflows but works for any Python application

docs.title: What Python versions are supported?
docs.text: minevent currently supports Python 3.11 and above. See the compatibility table in the README for specific version requirements.

docs.title: How do I install minevent?
docs.text:
The simplest way is via pip:

pip install minevent

For development or contributing, see the Get Started guide.

docs.title: Can I use minevent with other ML frameworks?
docs.text: Yes! minevent is framework-agnostic and can be integrated with PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn, or any other Python-based ML framework.

docs.title: How do I create a simple event handler?
docs.text:
from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager


def my_handler():
    print("Event triggered!")


manager = EventManager()
manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(my_handler))
manager.trigger_event("my_event")

docs.title: Can I pass arguments to event handlers?
docs.text:
Yes, use handler_args and handler_kwargs:

from minevent import EventHandler


def greet(name: str, greeting: str = "Hello"):
    print(f"{greeting}, {name}!")


handler = EventHandler(greet, handler_args=("Alice",), handler_kwargs={"greeting": "Hi"})
handler.handle()  # Prints: Hi, Alice!

docs.title: How do I execute a handler only sometimes?
docs.text:
Use EventHandler with a condition:

from minevent import EventHandler, PeriodicCondition

# Execute only every 5 times
handler = EventHandler(my_function, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=5))

docs.title: Can I add the same handler to multiple events?
docs.text:
Yes! You can register the same handler to different events:

handler = EventHandler(my_function)
manager.add_event_handler("event1", handler)
manager.add_event_handler("event2", handler)

docs.title: How do I remove an event handler?
docs.text:
Keep the Subscription returned by add_event_handler and call remove():

subscription = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", handler)
subscription.remove()  # True; False if it was already removed

A Subscription is a context manager, so with manager.add_event_handler(...): removes the registration when the block exits. manager.clear_event("my_event") removes all the handlers of an event.

docs.title: What happens if I trigger an event with no handlers?
docs.text: Nothing! The trigger_event method safely handles events with no registered handlers - it simply does nothing.

docs.title: Can I check if a handler is already registered?
docs.text:
Yes, look at the registrations of the event with get_subscriptions:

if not any(sub.event_handler is handler for sub in manager.get_subscriptions("my_event")):
    manager.add_event_handler("my_event", handler)

docs.title: Are event handlers executed in order?
docs.text: Yes! Event handlers are executed in the order they were registered using add_event_handler.

docs.title: Is minevent thread-safe?
docs.text: Partly. EventManager protects its registry with a lock, so you can register handlers in the main thread and trigger events from worker threads. The handlers run in the triggering thread, concurrently if several threads trigger the same event, and the counter of a stateful condition such as PeriodicCondition is not protected. See Thread Safety.

docs.title: Can I create custom conditions?
docs.text:
Yes! A condition is any function without argument that returns a boolean, so a lambda works. For a condition with a state, write a class with a __call__ method:

class MyCondition:
    def __call__(self) -> bool:
        # Your custom logic here
        return some_condition


handler = EventHandler(my_function, condition=MyCondition())

docs.title: Can I create custom event handlers?
docs.text:
Yes! Implement the BaseEventHandler class:

from minevent.handlers import BaseEventHandler


class MyEventHandler(BaseEventHandler):
    def handle(self, /, **payload: object) -> None:
        # Your custom logic here; payload holds the keyword arguments of trigger_event
        pass

docs.title: How do I integrate minevent into my training loop?
docs.text:
Here's a common pattern for ML training:

from minevent import EventManager, EventHandler


def train(epochs, manager):
    manager.trigger_event("training_start")

    for epoch in range(epochs):
        manager.trigger_event("epoch_start")

        # Training logic here
        for batch in data_loader:
            manager.trigger_event("batch_start")
            # Process batch
            manager.trigger_event("batch_end")

        manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")

    manager.trigger_event("training_end")


# Setup handlers
manager = EventManager()
manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", EventHandler(save_checkpoint))
manager.add_event_handler("training_end", EventHandler(log_metrics))

train(epochs=10, manager=manager)

docs.title: Can event handlers modify the event manager?
docs.text: Yes, but be cautious! An event handler can add or remove other handlers, but modifying the handlers of the currently firing event during its execution is not recommended as it may lead to unexpected behavior.

docs.title: What is the performance overhead of using minevent?
docs.text: minevent is designed to be lightweight with minimal overhead. The main cost is the function call overhead for each registered handler. For most ML workflows, this overhead is negligible compared to the computation time of training operations.

docs.title: I get "ValueError: event does not exist" when removing a handler
docs.text:
This means you're trying to remove a handler from an event that hasn't been registered. Make sure:

  1. The event name matches exactly (event names are case-sensitive)
  2. At least one handler has been added to that event before trying to remove one

docs.title: My handler isn't being called
docs.text:
Check that:

  1. You've registered the handler with add_event_handler
  2. You're triggering the correct event name (case-sensitive)
  3. If using a condition, the condition evaluates to True
  4. The handler function is callable and doesn't raise exceptions

docs.title: How do I debug event handlers?
docs.text:
Add logging to your handlers:

import logging


def my_handler():
    logging.info("Handler called")
    # Your logic here

Or check the event manager state:

print(manager)  # Shows the number of handlers of each event
print(manager.get_subscriptions("my_event"))  # Shows the registrations of an event

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The minevent event system is composed of three main components:

  • an event
  • an event handler
  • an event manager

It is a synchronous system i.e. only one event and event handler are executed at the same time. This page presents the design used in minevent, but other designs exist. The proposed design was not designed to work in all the scenarios, so it is highly recommended to read the documentation to understand if it fits your needs/requirements before to use it.

docs.title: Event
docs.text:
In minevent, an event is a string that represents something happening. The event is represented by the event name. For example, it is possible to write the following line to define an event that happens after the training is completed.

my_event = "training completed"

docs.title: Event handler
docs.text:
In minevent, an event handler is a piece a code that is executed when an even happened.

An event handler must have a handle method, which executes a piece of code when the event happens. Event handlers are compared by identity.

minevent provides EventHandler, which wraps a callable. It can take an optional condition to execute the logic only when the condition is true.

docs.title: Basic event handler
docs.text:
Let's assume we want to create an event handler to say hello when an event is fired. It is possible to implement this scenario as follow by using minvent.EventHandler.

>>> from minevent import EventHandler
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler)
>>> handler.handle()
Hello!

docs.title: Event handler with arguments
docs.text:
The previous example has no arguments. It is also possible to provide some arguments to customize the event handler. The arguments can be given as positional arguments using handler_args:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler
>>> def hello_handler(name: str, day: str) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello {name}! Happy {day}!")
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler, handler_args=("Bob", "Monday"))
>>> handler.handle()
Hello Bob! Happy Monday!

It is also possible to give the arguments as keyword arguments using handler_kwargs:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler
>>> def hello_handler(name: str, day: str) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello {name}! Happy {day}!")
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler, handler_kwargs={"name": "Bob", "day": "Monday"})
>>> handler.handle()
Hello Bob! Happy Monday!

It is also possible to use handler_args and handler_kwargs:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler
>>> def hello_handler(name: str, day: str) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello {name}! Happy {day}!")
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler, handler_args=["Bob"], handler_kwargs={"day": "Monday"})
>>> handler.handle()
Hello Bob! Happy Monday!

It is possible to define event handlers with a large range of functions. For example, it is possible to implement the same logic by using directly print:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler
>>> handler = EventHandler(print, handler_args=("Hello Bob! Happy Monday!",))
>>> handler.handle()
Hello Bob! Happy Monday!

docs.title: Event handler with condition
docs.text:
It is possible to define an event handler that is executed when a condition is true. The following example shows how to define an event handler where the logic is executed every three calls.

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, PeriodicCondition
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3))
>>> handler.handle()
Hello!
>>> handler.handle()
>>> handler.handle()
>>> handler.handle()
Hello!

PeriodicCondition is a condition implemented in minevent to execute an event handler with a periodic pattern. It is also possible to implement custom conditions. If the condition returns True, the logic associated to the event handler is executed, otherwise the logic associated to the event handler is not executed.

A plain function without argument that returns a boolean is also accepted as a condition:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> verbose = True
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler, condition=lambda: verbose)
>>> handler.handle()
Hello!

A condition is any function without argument that returns a boolean (the Condition protocol). minevent provides the stateful conditions OnceCondition (first call only), AfterNCondition (skip the first n calls) and PeriodicCondition(freq, skip_first=...). A class with a __call__ method is a condition too.

To combine conditions, write a function. You choose which conditions are evaluated:

>>> from minevent import AfterNCondition, EventHandler, PeriodicCondition
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> after_one, periodic = AfterNCondition(1), PeriodicCondition(2)
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler, condition=lambda: all([after_one(), periodic()]))
>>> for _ in range(5):
...     handler.handle()
Hello!
Hello!

all([a(), b()]) evaluates every condition at each call, so stateful conditions advance together. a() and b() skips b when a is False: use it when b is costly and stateless, because a stateful b would not count the calls skipped by a.

Stateful conditions (PeriodicCondition, OnceCondition, AfterNCondition) keep their counter in the instance. A condition instance given to two handlers is shared, so the two handlers advance the same counter. Create one instance per handler (a small factory function is enough):

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, PeriodicCondition
>>> def make_handler(name):
...     return EventHandler(print, handler_args=(name,), condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2))
>>> first, second = make_handler("first"), make_handler("second")
>>> first.handle()
first
>>> second.handle()
second

add_event_handler(..., once=True) and OnceCondition are two ways to run a handler once. Prefer once=True to run a handler on the next trigger of an event (the registration is removed). Use OnceCondition when the handler stays registered, for example inside a function that combines several conditions.

docs.title: Event handler identity
docs.text:
Event handlers are compared by identity: two EventHandlers created with the same arguments are different objects. To find or remove a registration, keep the Subscription returned by EventManager.add_event_handler (see Subscriptions).

>>> from minevent import EventHandler
>>> handler = EventHandler(print)
>>> handler == handler
True
>>> handler == EventHandler(print)
False

docs.title: Overview of the event manager
docs.text:
As explained by its name, the goal of the event manager is to manage event handlers. The event manager supports the following functionalities:

  • adding an event handler
  • firing all the event handlers associated to an event.
  • removing an event handler from an event

docs.title: Create an event manager
docs.text:
To use the event system, it is important to create an event manager. minevent implements an event manager, but it is possible to implement and use other compatible event managers. This documentation uses the default event manager implemented in minevent. To create an event manager, you can write:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> manager
EventManager(events={})

The representation of the event manager shows the number of event handlers of each event. The event manager is empty, so it shows there is no event handler.

docs.title: Add an event handler
docs.text:
This section describes how to add an event handler to an event manager. The method to add an event handler to the event manager is add_event_handler. There are several approaches to add an event handler.

The simplest approach requires an event and an event handler. The following example shows how to add a hello_handler handler to the 'my_event' event.

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})

You can see there is a registered event handler for the event name my_event.

It is possible to add an event handler that takes some input arguments. The following example shows how to add an event handler with some positional arguments.

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler(first_name: str, last_name: str) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello. I am {last_name}, {first_name} {last_name}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler, ("John", "Smith")))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler, ("Jane", "Doe")))
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 2})

For a given event, the event handlers are ordered by using the order of addition. The event handler (0) was added before the event handler (1). Internally, each event uses a list to store the registered event handlers. It is possible to add the same event handler multiple times:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 2})

docs.title: Subscriptions
docs.text:
add_event_handler returns a Subscription, the registration of the handler. Its remove() method removes exactly that registration, even if the same handler is registered several times, and returns False if it was already removed:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler)
>>> first = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", handler)
>>> second = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", handler)
>>> first.remove()
True
>>> first.remove()
False
>>> second.active
True
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!

get_subscriptions returns the registrations of an event, in the order the handlers run, and len(manager) is the total number of registrations. If you want to add an event handler only once, check the registrations:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler)
>>> for _ in range(5):
...     if not any(s.event_handler is handler for s in manager.get_subscriptions("my_event")):
...         _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", handler)
>>> len(manager)
1

To run a handler only on the next trigger, use once=True:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler), once=True)
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")

once=True means "the next trigger", not "the next time the handler runs": the registration is removed on the next trigger even if the condition of the EventHandler is False and the function is not called. If you need the handler to run the first time its condition is True, register it without once and use OnceCondition as the condition.

A Subscription is a context manager that removes the registration when the block exits, and its active property tells if the handler is still registered. EventManager.on is a decorator that registers a function and returns it unchanged:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> with manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(print, handler_args=("Hello!",))) as sub:
...     manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> sub.active
False
>>> @manager.on("epoch_end")
... def log_epoch(epoch):
...     print(f"epoch {epoch}")
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", epoch=1)
epoch 1

docs.title: Fire an event
docs.text:
This section describes how to fire an event. As explained above, it is possible to add a handler to an event. Then, we want to execute the handler when the event is fired. The following example shows how to fire the hello_handler for the event 'my_event':

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})

You can note that the last fired event name has been updated. The current last fired event name is 'my_event'. The event manager uses the arguments that were given when the event handler was added.

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler(first_name: str, last_name: str) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello. I am {first_name} {last_name}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler, ("John", "Smith")))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler, ("Jane", "Doe")))
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 2})
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello. I am John Smith
Hello. I am Jane Doe

As explained above, it is possible to add a condition to control when to execute the handler. The following shows how to execute the hello_handler every 3 'my_event' events.

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, PeriodicCondition, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3))
... )
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})
>>> for i in range(10):
...     print(f"i={i}")
...     manager.trigger_event("my_event")
i=0
Hello!
i=1
i=2
i=3
Hello!
i=4
i=5
i=6
Hello!
i=7
i=8
i=9
Hello!

The trigger_event method does nothing if there is no event handler registered for the event:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")

docs.title: Share an event between handlers that need different payload keys
docs.text:
Every handler receives the whole payload, so a handler that does not accept a key raises a TypeError. Either accept the extra keys with **_, or create the handler with filter_payload=True to pass only the keys its signature accepts:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def log_loss(loss):
...     print(f"loss {loss}")
>>> def log_epoch(epoch):
...     print(f"epoch {epoch}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", EventHandler(log_loss, filter_payload=True))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", EventHandler(log_epoch, filter_payload=True))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", epoch=3, loss=0.5)
loss 0.5
epoch 3

docs.title: Fire an event with coroutine handlers
docs.text:
trigger_event calls the handlers synchronously and raises a TypeError for a coroutine function (the coroutine would never be awaited). To use coroutine handlers, fire the event with atrigger_event, which awaits the coroutines (and also runs synchronous handlers) one after the other, in the order they were added:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> async def hello_handler(name: str) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello {name}!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("my_event", name="John"))
Hello John!

docs.title: Remove an event handler
docs.text:
A previous section describes how to add an event handler, but sometimes it is useful to remove an event handler. Call remove() on the Subscription returned by add_event_handler:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> subscription = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})
>>> subscription.remove()
True
>>> manager
EventManager(events={})

If you did not keep the subscription, get_subscriptions returns the registrations of an event, and clear_event removes all the event handlers of an event:

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(print))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_other_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> manager.get_subscriptions("my_event")[0].remove()
True
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1, 'my_other_event': 1})
>>> manager.clear_event("my_event")
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_other_event': 1})

docs.title: Reset the event manager
docs.text:
It is possible to reset the event manager with the reset method. It removes all the event handlers and makes their subscriptions inactive. It is equivalent to create a new event manager.

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_other_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1, 'my_other_event': 1})
>>> manager.reset()
>>> manager
EventManager(events={})

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: This guide helps you diagnose and resolve common issues when using minevent.

docs.title: Event Handler Not Executing
docs.text:
Symptoms: You trigger an event but the handler doesn't execute.

Possible Causes and Solutions:

  1. Handler not registered
# Check the registrations of the event
print(manager.get_subscriptions("my_event"))  # () if no handler is registered
print("my_event" in manager)
  1. Wrong event name (event names are case-sensitive)
# These are different events!
manager.add_event_handler("MyEvent", handler)
manager.trigger_event("myevent")  # Won't trigger - different case!

# Solution: Use consistent naming
EVENT_NAME = "my_event"
manager.add_event_handler(EVENT_NAME, handler)
manager.trigger_event(EVENT_NAME)
  1. Conditional handler condition is False
# Check condition state
condition = PeriodicCondition(freq=5)
handler = EventHandler(my_function, condition=condition)

# The handler only executes every 5 calls
for i in range(10):
    manager.trigger_event("my_event")
    print(f"Call {i}: Condition evaluated to {condition()}")
  1. Handler raises an exception
# Add error handling to debug
def safe_handler():
    try:
        my_function()
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Handler error: {e}")
        import traceback

        traceback.print_exc()


manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(safe_handler))

docs.title: Removing a Handler That Is Already Removed
docs.text:
Symptoms: subscription.remove() returns False.

Cause: The registration was already removed: by remove(), by clear_event or reset, or because it was registered with once=True and the event was triggered.

Solution: This is not an error. Use subscription.active to check if the handler is still registered.

docs.title: Cannot Find a Handler to Remove
docs.text:
Symptoms: You did not keep the Subscription returned by add_event_handler.

Cause: Event handlers are compared by identity, so a new EventHandler built with the same arguments is a different object.

Solution: Look at the registrations of the event and remove the one you want:

for subscription in manager.get_subscriptions("my_event"):
    if subscription.event_handler.handler is my_function:
        subscription.remove()

docs.title: Memory Leaks
docs.text:
Symptoms: Memory usage grows over time in long-running applications.

Cause: A registered handler stays alive as long as the manager does. EventHandler(obj.method) keeps obj alive, and so do handler_args and closures. minevent does not use weak references (see the non-goals in the architecture page), so unsubscribe handlers you no longer need.

Solution:

# Keep the Subscription and remove it when the owner is done
subscription = manager.add_event_handler("event", EventHandler(obj.method))
# Later...
subscription.remove()  # `obj` can be garbage collected


# Or scope the registration to a block
with manager.add_event_handler("event", EventHandler(obj.method)):
    run_phase()

# Clear all the handlers of an event, or of the manager
manager.clear_event("event")
manager.reset()

If a handler must not keep an object alive, give it a weakref and do nothing when the object is gone:

import weakref


def make_handler(large_object):
    ref = weakref.ref(large_object)

    def handle():
        obj = ref()
        if obj is not None:
            ...  # Use the object

    return EventHandler(handle)


subscription = manager.add_event_handler("event", make_handler(large_object))

The handler itself stays registered (and cheap) until you remove it.

docs.title: Unexpected Handler Execution Order
docs.text:
Symptoms: Handlers execute in unexpected order.

Cause: Handlers execute in the order they were registered.

Solution:

# Handlers execute in registration order
manager.add_event_handler("event", EventHandler(first_handler))  # Executes 1st
manager.add_event_handler("event", EventHandler(second_handler))  # Executes 2nd
manager.add_event_handler("event", EventHandler(third_handler))  # Executes 3rd


# If order matters, register in correct order
# Or use a single handler that calls functions in desired order
def orchestrator():
    first_handler()
    second_handler()
    third_handler()


manager.add_event_handler("event", EventHandler(orchestrator))

docs.title: Slow Event Triggering
docs.text:
Symptoms: trigger_event takes a long time.

Possible Causes:

  1. Too many handlers registered
# Check number of handlers
print(f"Manager state: {manager}")


# Reduce handlers by combining related operations
def combined_handler():
    operation1()
    operation2()
    operation3()


manager.add_event_handler("event", EventHandler(combined_handler))
  1. Handlers performing heavy computation
# Profile handler execution time
import time


def timed_handler():
    start = time.time()
    actual_handler()
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    if elapsed > 0.1:
        print(f"Handler took {elapsed:.2f}s")


# Move heavy work to background thread
import concurrent.futures

executor = concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor()


def async_handler():
    executor.submit(heavy_computation)


manager.add_event_handler("event", EventHandler(async_handler))
  1. Frequent condition evaluation
# Use PeriodicCondition to reduce execution frequency
from minevent import EventHandler, PeriodicCondition

# Instead of executing every time
manager.add_event_handler("frequent_event", EventHandler(expensive_handler))

# Execute less frequently
manager.add_event_handler(
    "frequent_event",
    EventHandler(expensive_handler, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=10)),
)

docs.title: Enable Logging
docs.text:
import logging

# Enable debug logging for minevent
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)
logger = logging.getLogger("minevent")
logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)

# Now minevent will log when handlers are added/removed/triggered
manager = EventManager()
manager.add_event_handler("event", EventHandler(my_handler))
manager.trigger_event("event")

docs.title: Inspect Event Manager State
docs.text:
# Print the number of handlers of each event
print(manager)

# List the registrations of an event
print(manager.get_subscriptions("my_event"))

# Check if an event has handlers
print("my_event" in manager)

docs.title: Add Debugging Handlers
docs.text:
# Add a debug handler that logs all events
def debug_handler(event_name):
    print(f"DEBUG: Event '{event_name}' triggered")


# Register for multiple events
for event in ["event1", "event2", "event3"]:
    manager.add_event_handler(event, EventHandler(debug_handler, handler_args=(event,)))

docs.title: Handlers Not Called in Tests
docs.text:
Cause: Event manager not properly set up in test fixtures.

Solution:

import pytest
from minevent import EventManager, EventHandler


@pytest.fixture
def manager():
    """Create a fresh event manager for each test."""
    mgr = EventManager()
    yield mgr
    mgr.reset()  # Clean up after test


def test_handler_execution(manager):
    """Test that handler is called."""
    called = []

    def test_handler():
        called.append(True)

    manager.add_event_handler("test_event", EventHandler(test_handler))
    manager.trigger_event("test_event")

    assert len(called) == 1

docs.title: Mocking Handlers
docs.text:
from unittest.mock import Mock


def test_with_mock():
    """Test using mock handlers."""
    manager = EventManager()
    mock_handler = Mock()

docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Define the protocol of a condition for EventHandler.

A condition is any function without argument that returns a boolean: a lambda, a method, or an object with a __call__ method like the conditions of this module. It is called each time the event is triggered, before the handler, and the handler is executed only if it returns True. A condition can keep a state between calls.

To combine conditions, write a function. The function decides which conditions are evaluated: lambda: a() and b() skips b when a is False, while lambda: all([a(), b()]) evaluates both, so stateful conditions advance together.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventHandler, PeriodicCondition
>>> condition = PeriodicCondition(freq=3)
>>> handler = EventHandler(print, ["Hello!"], condition=condition)
>>> handler.handle()
Hello!
>>> handler.handle()
>>> handler = EventHandler(print, ["Bye!"], condition=lambda: False)
>>> handler.handle()

docs.title: minevent.EventHandler
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEventHandler

Implement an event handler.

This class wraps a callable function or method and allows it to be executed as an event handler. The handler can be configured with positional and keyword arguments that will be passed when the handler is executed, and with an optional condition. When a condition is given, the handler is executed only if the condition evaluates to True. This is useful for scenarios where event handlers should only run under specific circumstances, such as periodic execution or state-based triggering.

The handler is called as handler(*handler_args, **handler_kwargs, **payload), where payload is the data given when the event is triggered.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default handler Callable[..., object]

The callable function or method to be invoked when the event is triggered (and the condition is True).

required handler_args Sequence[Any] | None

The positional arguments to pass to the handler when it is called. Default is None.

None handler_kwargs Mapping[str, Any] | None

The keyword arguments to pass to the handler when it is called. The dictionary is copied, so changing it afterwards does not change the handler. Default is None.

None condition Condition | None

The condition that controls whether the handler is executed: a function without argument that returns a boolean, such as a lambda or a PeriodicCondition. It is called each time the event is triggered, before the handler. If None, the handler is always executed. Default is None.

None filter_payload bool

If True, only the payload keys that the signature of the handler accepts are passed to it, so handlers with different needs can share an event without **kwargs. The accepted keys are computed once, at construction. A handler with a **kwargs parameter, or whose signature cannot be inspected, receives the whole payload. Keys of handler_kwargs are not filtered. Default is False.

False

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if handler is not callable, if handler_args is a str or bytes (which would be split into characters), or if condition is neither None nor callable.

>>> from minevent import EventHandler, PeriodicCondition
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler)
>>> handler
EventHandler(handler=<function hello_handler at 0x...>, handler_args=(), handler_kwargs={}, condition=None, filter_payload=False)
>>> handler.handle()
Hello!
>>> handler = EventHandler(print, handler_args=["Hello!"])
>>> handler.handle()
Hello!
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3))
>>> handler

Hello!
>>> handler.handle()
>>> handler.handle()
>>> handler.handle()
Hello!
>>> def epoch_handler(epoch: int) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {epoch}")
...
>>> handler = EventHandler(epoch_handler, filter_payload=True)
>>> handler.handle(epoch=3, loss=0.5)

docs.title: minevent.EventManager
docs.text:
Implement an event manager.

This event manager allows registering event handlers and triggering events. An event is represented by a case-sensitive string. Each event can have multiple handlers attached, and all handlers are executed in the order they were added when the event is triggered.

Error policy: handlers run fail-fast. If a handler raises, the exception propagates to the caller of trigger_event and the remaining handlers of that event are not executed.

Thread safety: the registration, removal and inspection of handlers are protected by a reentrant lock, and trigger_event runs the handlers on a snapshot taken under the lock, outside of it. So handlers can be registered in one thread and events triggered from worker threads. The handlers themselves run in the thread that triggers the event, concurrently if several threads trigger the same event, so a handler that shares state must be thread-safe. The mutable state of a condition, such as the counter of PeriodicCondition, is not protected.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler():
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!

docs.text:
trigger_event(event: str, /, **payload: object) -> None

Trigger the handler(s) for the given event.

This method executes all event handlers registered for the specified event in the order they were added. The last triggered event name is updated regardless of whether any handlers are registered.

Handlers are executed fail-fast: if a handler raises, the exception propagates and the remaining handlers are skipped. The exception is not wrapped: it has a note (__notes__) with the event and the handler that raised it.

The handlers are read from a snapshot taken when the event is triggered. Handlers added or removed by a running handler take effect on the next trigger, not the current one.

A handler can trigger events, including the event it handles, but nothing stops the recursion: a handler that always triggers its own event raises a RecursionError. Guard the recursive trigger with a condition or a flag.

The keyword arguments payload are passed to every handler as keyword arguments, after the arguments given at registration. Without payload, handlers are called exactly as before. A handler that does not accept the payload raises a TypeError. The payload can use any key, including event and self, because event is positional-only.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default event str

The event name (case-sensitive string) to trigger.

required **payload object

The data passed to the handlers as keyword arguments.

{}

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if event is not a string.

>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")  # do nothing because there is no event handler
>>> def hello_handler():
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> def epoch_handler(epoch):
...     print(f"epoch {epoch}")
...

>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", epoch=3)

docs.title: minevent.PeriodicCondition
docs.text:
Implement a periodic condition.

This condition evaluates to True on the first call and then every freq calls. It maintains an internal counter that increments with each call. The condition is True when the counter modulo freq equals zero.

Note that a call is not idempotent: each call advances the counter, so the condition is stateful. Do not share one instance between several handlers, because they would advance the same counter. Use reset to restart the counter. The counter is not protected by a lock, so a condition should be called from one thread.

The frequency (interval) at which the condition evaluates to True. Must be a positive integer.

required skip_first bool

If True, the first call evaluates to False, and then the condition evaluates to True every freq calls. Default is False.

False

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if freq is not an integer.

ValueError

if freq is lower than 1.

Example 
>>> from minevent import PeriodicCondition
>>> condition = PeriodicCondition(freq=3)
>>> [condition() for _ in range(7)]
[True, False, False, True, False, False, True]
>>> condition = PeriodicCondition(freq=2, skip_first=True)
>>> [condition() for _ in range(3)]
[False, False, True]

Represent the registration of an event handler to an event.

A subscription is returned by EventManager.add_event_handler. It is the registration itself: the manager stores it, and it removes exactly the registration that created it. The handler does not need to be re-created to be unsubscribed, other registrations of the same handler are not removed, and registering the same handler twice creates two independent subscriptions.

A subscription is a context manager: the registration is removed when the with block exits.

The constructor is internal: subscriptions are created by the event manager.

required event str

required once bool

False Example 
>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> subscription = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(print))
>>> subscription.event
'my_event'
>>> subscription.active
True
>>> subscription.remove()
True
>>> subscription.remove()
False
>>> subscription.active
False
>>> manager.events
[]
>>> with manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(print)):
...     manager.events
...
['my_event']
>>> manager.events
[]

docs.title: minevent.handlers.EventHandler
docs.text:
Bases: BaseEventHandler

Implement an event handler.

This class wraps a callable function or method and allows it to be executed as an event handler. The handler can be configured with positional and keyword arguments that will be passed when the handler is executed, and with an optional condition. When a condition is given, the handler is executed only if the condition evaluates to True. This is useful for scenarios where event handlers should only run under specific circumstances, such as periodic execution or state-based triggering.

The handler is called as handler(*handler_args, **handler_kwargs, **payload), where payload is the data given when the event is triggered.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default handler Callable[..., object]

The callable function or method to be invoked when the event is triggered (and the condition is True).

required handler_args Sequence[Any] | None

The positional arguments to pass to the handler when it is called. Default is None.

None handler_kwargs Mapping[str, Any] | None

The keyword arguments to pass to the handler when it is called. The dictionary is copied, so changing it afterwards does not change the handler. Default is None.

None condition Condition | None

The condition that controls whether the handler is executed: a function without argument that returns a boolean, such as a lambda or a PeriodicCondition. It is called each time the event is triggered, before the handler. If None, the handler is always executed. Default is None.

None filter_payload bool

If True, only the payload keys that the signature of the handler accepts are passed to it, so handlers with different needs can share an event without **kwargs. The accepted keys are computed once, at construction. A handler with a **kwargs parameter, or whose signature cannot be inspected, receives the whole payload. Keys of handler_kwargs are not filtered. Default is False.

False

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if handler is not callable, if handler_args is a str or bytes (which would be split into characters), or if condition is neither None nor callable.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventHandler, PeriodicCondition
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler)
>>> handler
EventHandler(handler=<function hello_handler at 0x...>, handler_args=(), handler_kwargs={}, condition=None, filter_payload=False)
>>> handler.handle()
Hello!
>>> handler = EventHandler(print, handler_args=["Hello!"])
>>> handler.handle()
Hello!
>>> handler = EventHandler(hello_handler, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3))
>>> handler
EventHandler(handler=<function hello_handler at 0x...>, handler_args=(), handler_kwargs={}, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3, skip_first=False, step=0), filter_payload=False)
>>> handler.handle()
Hello!
>>> handler.handle()
>>> handler.handle()
>>> handler.handle()
Hello!
>>> def epoch_handler(epoch: int) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {epoch}")
...
>>> handler = EventHandler(epoch_handler, filter_payload=True)
>>> handler.handle(epoch=3, loss=0.5)
epoch 3

docs.title: minevent.manager.EventManager
docs.text:
Implement an event manager.

This event manager allows registering event handlers and triggering events. An event is represented by a case-sensitive string. Each event can have multiple handlers attached, and all handlers are executed in the order they were added when the event is triggered.

Error policy: handlers run fail-fast. If a handler raises, the exception propagates to the caller of trigger_event and the remaining handlers of that event are not executed.

Thread safety: the registration, removal and inspection of handlers are protected by a reentrant lock, and trigger_event runs the handlers on a snapshot taken under the lock, outside of it. So handlers can be registered in one thread and events triggered from worker threads. The handlers themselves run in the thread that triggers the event, concurrently if several threads trigger the same event, so a handler that shares state must be thread-safe. The mutable state of a condition, such as the counter of PeriodicCondition, is not protected.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler():
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!

docs.text:
trigger_event(event: str, /, **payload: object) -> None

Trigger the handler(s) for the given event.

This method executes all event handlers registered for the specified event in the order they were added. The last triggered event name is updated regardless of whether any handlers are registered.

Handlers are executed fail-fast: if a handler raises, the exception propagates and the remaining handlers are skipped. The exception is not wrapped: it has a note (__notes__) with the event and the handler that raised it.

The handlers are read from a snapshot taken when the event is triggered. Handlers added or removed by a running handler take effect on the next trigger, not the current one.

A handler can trigger events, including the event it handles, but nothing stops the recursion: a handler that always triggers its own event raises a RecursionError. Guard the recursive trigger with a condition or a flag.

The keyword arguments payload are passed to every handler as keyword arguments, after the arguments given at registration. Without payload, handlers are called exactly as before. A handler that does not accept the payload raises a TypeError. The payload can use any key, including event and self, because event is positional-only.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default event str

The event name (case-sensitive string) to trigger.

required **payload object

The data passed to the handlers as keyword arguments.

{}

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if event is not a string.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventHandler, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")  # do nothing because there is no event handler
>>> def hello_handler():
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", EventHandler(hello_handler))
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> def epoch_handler(epoch):
...     print(f"epoch {epoch}")
...
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", EventHandler(epoch_handler))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", epoch=3)
epoch 3
